title: Sky light: option 2 vs option 3, blind
question: Can you tell these two apart at all? If you can, which one reads better as a pit — and is that difference worth the machinery the costs below describe?
context_md:
Same world, same seed, same 64-wide pit, same model and constants. **The only difference is where the answer is computed and stored.** Blinded because I have a stake — I recommended one of them before testing the other.

**Option 2 — coarse grid, recomputed per frame over the viewport.** Block size 4, four directional sweeps twice, bilinear per pixel. No stored state, no invalidation; recompute and it is right by construction. **This is what is in the app on F12 right now.**

**Option 3 — per-pixel field over the whole world, stored and maintained incrementally.** You asked whether I had tested this. I had not — I had measured per-pixel *recomputed from scratch*, which is a different thing, and the difference is the whole of the risk. Now tested.

### Option 3 works, including the hard direction

Light *rises* when you dig (a relax handles it) and *falls* when you fill, which a max-propagation cannot undo locally. Four edits, the last plugging the mouth of a lit shaft so a hundred rows below had been lit *through* the filled cell. Each checked against a full recompute, not against a cheaper version of itself — worst error 0.0005, 0.0005, 0.0005, 0.0029, all under the 1/255 = 0.0039 visibility floor.

The mechanism is a bounded local re-solve rather than the classic light-removal BFS: zero everything within a radius, treat the ring outside as fixed sources, re-solve the interior. Correct because a cell's light is at most 0.91^d of any source d cells away *along the path*, and a path is never shorter than the straight line. Swept rather than asserted, because a theory predicting "just under threshold" and a measurement landing just under it are the same number twice:

| radius | worst error | vs 0.0039 |
|---|---|---|
| 30 | 0.0381 | **visible, 10x over** |
| 59 (theoretical minimum) | 0.0029 | just under |
| 90 | 0.0007 | comfortable |

### The cost, and it reverses the intuition

Incremental is supposed to be the cheap one. It is not, because its bill scales with **how many separate places changed** and option 2's does not:

| | cost on a frame where something changed |
|---|---|
| **option 2** | **2.3 ms flat** — however violent the frame |
| **option 3**, radius 59 | **0.7 ms per edit site** |
| **option 3**, radius 90 (the safe one) | **~1.6 ms per edit site** |

So option 3 is cheaper only below ~3 edit sites per frame, ~1.5 at the radius it should actually use. A falling-sand world does not oblige — 16 of 40 chunks awake on a collapse, 40 of 40 while terrain settles.

### What option 3 buys that option 2 cannot

- **Panning over a still world.** Its field is world-space, so a camera move costs nothing; option 2 recomputes on every one.
- **Anything off-screen that needs a correct answer** — creature sight, plant siting, a minimap. Option 2 only ever knows the viewport.

Against: 1.3 MB at 2048x640, a ~45 ms genesis solve, and one obligation option 2 does not have at all — **every** cell change must be caught, including ones the CA makes on its own. Miss a falling grain and the stale bright patch is permanent, because nothing ever recomputes it. Same class as the stateful skyline in dead-ends.md §985.

Full write-up in `Reports/sky-light-design.md`.
